plan.title: Zero Velocity at the Top Is Not Zero Acceleration
plan.story:
Maya tosses a tennis ball straight up from her hand. For a moment at the top it seems to hang in the air. Her friend Theo says: "Right there the ball is stopped, so nothing is acting on it. Its acceleration must be zero." It sounds reasonable. If something is not moving, what could be changing?

To test Theo's idea, we need to keep two words apart. Velocity says how fast the ball moves and in which direction. Upward counts as positive here. Acceleration says how fast the velocity itself is changing, in metres per second gained or lost every second (m/s²). Being zero and changing are two different things. A car's speedometer can pass through zero while the car is changing from reversing to driving forward.

Let us work through an example. Ignore air resistance and say Maya throws the ball upward at 9.8 m/s. Near Earth's surface gravity pulls the ball down, and on its own this changes the velocity by 9.8 m/s downward every second. We call this g = 9.8 m/s².

Follow the ball second by second. At launch (t = 0 s) the velocity is +9.8 m/s. After 0.5 s it has lost 4.9 m/s, so it is +4.9 m/s, and the ball is 3.675 m above her hand. At t = 1.0 s it has lost 9.8 m/s in total, so the velocity is exactly 0. This is the top, 4.9 m up. At t = 1.5 s the velocity is -4.9 m/s. The ball is back at 3.675 m, the same height as at 0.5 s, but now it is moving down. At t = 2.0 s it reaches her hand again at -9.8 m/s.

Look at the pattern. Every half-second the velocity drops by the same 4.9 m/s, before the top, across the top and after it. Plot velocity against time and you get one straight line that slopes down and crosses zero without bending. The slope of that line is the acceleration, -9.8 m/s². The line has the same slope where it crosses zero as everywhere else.

Now zoom in on the top. At t = 0.9 s the velocity is +0.98 m/s, still slightly upward. At t = 1.1 s it is -0.98 m/s, slightly downward. In those 0.2 s the velocity changed by -1.96 m/s, and -1.96 divided by 0.2 is -9.8 m/s². The velocity is passing through zero, and it is changing just as quickly as ever while it does.

Here is a thought experiment that settles it. Suppose Theo were right and the acceleration really were zero at the top. Zero acceleration means the velocity stops changing. The ball would keep its velocity of zero and hang in the air forever. Balls do not do that. The ball only turns round because something keeps changing its velocity at the top. Gravity has not switched off. The ball's weight pulls on it the whole time, so by Newton's second law it accelerates downward the whole time.

Galileo reached the same picture in the early 1600s. His experiments with balls rolling down ramps, comparing distances travelled in successive times, led him to conclude that the speed of a freely moving body changes by equal amounts in equal times. A thrown ball is the same uniform change, starting from an upward velocity.

So, back to Maya's ball. At the highest point the velocity is zero only for an instant, as the velocity passes from positive to negative. The acceleration is not zero. It is 9.8 m/s² downward, the same as at every other moment of the flight. Zero velocity tells you where the ball is turning round. The constant downward acceleration is what makes it turn round.
plan.cardDescription: Follow a ball thrown straight up: velocity shrinks to zero at the top, yet the downward 9.8 m/s² acceleration never vanishes. No air resistance.
plan.learningGoal: Explain, using the slope of the velocity-time line and the constant downward acceleration arrow, why a vertically thrown ball has zero velocity but an acceleration of 9.8 m/s² downward at its highest point.

scene.description: Left panel: vertical height axis 0 to 5 m, origin at the release hand (h = 0), up positive, gridlines every 1 m, dashed peak line at 4.9 m. The ball moves on a vertical path. Ghost dots every 0.25 s appear only up to the current time; rising ghosts are filled, falling ghosts are hollow and offset slightly right. A blue velocity arrow on the ball, scaled 0.1 m per 1 m/s, points up or down. A red acceleration arrow on its own fixed scale always points down with the same length, labelled 9.8 m/s². Right panel: velocity-time plot, 0 to 2 s and -10 to +10 m/s, with a zero line, the faint full line v = 9.8 - 9.8t and a bright trace with a moving dot. A slope triangle at the dot, clamped inside the plot, reads 'slope = -9.8 m/s²'. A vertical time cursor shares the ball's clock. Readouts: time, height, velocity, acceleration, rounded half away from zero to 2 decimals after adding a tiny epsilon, with -0.00 shown as 0.00. At the peak the velocity readout shows 0.00 m/s and the red arrow is unchanged.

entities.label: Ball
entities.purpose: The thrown ball; its vertical position shows height at the current time.

entities.label: Height axis
entities.purpose: Vertical scale 0 to 5 m from the release hand, with a dashed peak line at 4.9 m.

entities.label: Position ghosts
entities.purpose: Dots every 0.25 s, shown only up to the current time, revealing that the ball covers less distance per interval near the top. Rising ghosts are filled; falling ghosts are hollow and offset slightly right so both halves of the flight stay distinguishable.

entities.label: Velocity arrow
entities.purpose: Blue arrow on the ball whose length and direction show the current velocity; it shrinks to nothing at the top and then flips downward.

entities.label: Acceleration arrow
entities.purpose: Red arrow on the ball that always points down with the same length, showing that the 9.8 m/s² acceleration is constant, including at the top.

entities.label: Velocity-time plot
entities.purpose: Plot of velocity from -10 to +10 m/s against time from 0 to 2 s, with a zero line, the full straight line drawn faint and a bright trace up to the current time.

entities.label: Slope triangle
entities.purpose: Small rise-over-run triangle at the current point on the plot, labelled with slope -9.8 m/s², the same at every time.

entities.label: Time cursor
entities.purpose: Vertical line on the plot at the current time, linked to the ball's position.

quantities.label: Time
quantities.meaning: Elapsed time since the ball leaves the hand.
quantities.reference: Zero at release; the timeline runs 0 to 2 s.

quantities.label: Height
quantities.meaning: Height of the ball above the release hand.
quantities.reference: Zero at the hand, upward positive.
quantities.relation: h equals v0 times t minus one half of g times t squared.

quantities.label: Velocity
quantities.meaning: Vertical velocity of the ball, positive upward.
quantities.relation: v equals v0 minus g times t.

quantities.label: Acceleration
quantities.meaning: Rate of change of velocity; constant at -9.8 m/s², meaning 9.8 m/s² downward.
quantities.reference: Upward positive, so downward acceleration is negative.
quantities.relation: a equals minus g at every time, including the peak.

quantities.label: Launch speed
quantities.meaning: Upward velocity at release, fixed at 9.8 m/s.

quantities.label: Gravitational acceleration
quantities.meaning: Size of the downward acceleration from gravity, fixed at 9.8 m/s².
quantities.reference: Near Earth's surface, no air resistance.

observations.text: The red acceleration arrow keeps the same downward length at launch, on the way up, at the peak and on the way down, while the acceleration readout stays at -9.8 m/s².
The blue velocity arrow shrinks, vanishes at t = 1.0 s with the velocity readout at 0.00 m/s, then grows pointing down. The velocity passes through zero and does not stay there.
The velocity-time trace is one straight line crossing zero at t = 1.0 s without bending; the slope triangle reads -9.8 m/s² at every time, including the crossing.
At t = 0.5 s and t = 1.5 s the height readout shows 3.68 m both times, but the velocity is +4.9 m/s and then -4.9 m/s, so the blue arrows point opposite ways.

checkpoints.label: Launch
checkpoints.expected: Ball at h = 0 m, long blue arrow up (+9.8 m/s), red arrow down at 9.8 m/s², plot dot at (0 s, +9.8 m/s).

checkpoints.label: Rising
checkpoints.expected: h = 3.68 m, v = +4.9 m/s with a half-length blue arrow up, red arrow unchanged, a = -9.8 m/s².

checkpoints.label: Just before peak
checkpoints.expected: h = 4.85 m, v = +0.98 m/s with a short blue arrow up, red arrow unchanged at full length, a = -9.8 m/s².

checkpoints.label: Peak
checkpoints.expected: h = 4.9 m on the dashed peak line, v = 0.00 m/s with no blue arrow, red arrow still down at full length, a = -9.8 m/s², plot dot on the zero line and slope still -9.8 m/s².

checkpoints.label: Just after peak
checkpoints.expected: h = 4.85 m, v = -0.98 m/s with a short blue arrow down, red arrow unchanged at full length, a = -9.8 m/s².

checkpoints.label: Falling
checkpoints.expected: h = 3.68 m again, v = -4.9 m/s with a half-length blue arrow down, red arrow unchanged.

checkpoints.label: Back at hand
checkpoints.expected: h = 0 m, v = -9.8 m/s with a long blue arrow down, red arrow unchanged, plot trace complete as one straight line.

mode.initialState: Paused at t = 0 s. The ball sits at the release hand (h = 0 m) with a long blue velocity arrow pointing up (+9.8 m/s) and the red acceleration arrow pointing down (9.8 m/s²). The velocity-time plot shows the faint full line, with the dot at (0 s, +9.8 m/s). Readouts show t = 0.00 s, h = 0.00 m, v = +9.80 m/s and a = -9.80 m/s².

controls.label: Play
controls.purpose: Run the flight from release to return at half speed so the learner can watch the velocity arrow shrink, vanish and flip while the acceleration arrow stays the same.
controls.selectionReason: The answer depends on how velocity changes over time, so the learner needs to watch the timeline run. Play shows the motion continuously, which a single still view cannot.

controls.label: Time since release
controls.purpose: Seek to any instant from 0 to 2 s, especially just before, at and just after the peak, and compare the readouts and arrows.
controls.selectionReason: Stopping exactly at the peak and at 0.9 s and 1.1 s is the key comparison. Playback alone moves too quickly through that instant.

assumptions: Air resistance is ignored, so gravity is the only force on the ball after release.
g is taken as 9.8 m/s², constant over the 4.9 m height range.
The ball is released at h = 0 with an upward velocity of 9.8 m/s and caught again at the same height.
Upward is positive, so the constant acceleration is recorded as -9.8 m/s².
limitations: The launch speed is fixed. The learner cannot test other speeds, although the acceleration would be the same for any launch speed in this model.
The scene does not show the throw while the ball is still in the hand, when the hand's push also acts on it.
With real air drag the acceleration would be slightly larger than g on the way up and smaller on the way down. It would still not be zero at the top, but the scene does not show this.

claims.text: With launch velocity 9.8 m/s and g = 9.8 m/s², the velocity reaches zero at t = 1.0 s at a height of 4.9 m.
At t = 0.5 s and t = 1.5 s the ball is at 3.675 m with velocities +4.9 m/s and -4.9 m/s.
Across the peak, the velocity changes from +0.98 m/s at 0.9 s to -0.98 m/s at 1.1 s, an average acceleration of -9.8 m/s².
The ball returns to the hand at t = 2.0 s with velocity -9.8 m/s.
Without air resistance, the only force after release is the ball's weight, so by Newton's second law the acceleration is g downward at every instant, including the peak.
claims.check: a = F/m = mg/m = g, independent of velocity; the velocity-time line has a constant slope of -9.8 m/s².

claims.text: Galileo's ramp experiments in the early 1600s, comparing distances travelled in successive times, led him to conclude that freely moving bodies change speed by equal amounts in equal times.
claims.check: No evidence was supplied. This is a widely taught historical point and the story relies on it only for background. A history-of-science source such as Galileo's Two New Sciences (1638) would confirm it.

open: Claim cGalileo (ramp experiments led Galileo to conclude equal speed changes in equal times) has no supplied evidence. It is background only and does not affect the physics conclusion.
carried: Confirm that falling ghosts (hollow, offset right) are distinguishable from rising ones at t = 2 s, and that the slope triangle stays inside the plot and readable near t = 0 and t = 2 s.
Confirm that the velocity and acceleration arrows at h = 0 are not clipped, and that the separate scales for the red and blue arrows do not invite a misleading comparison of their lengths.
